items.reason: Administrative closeout checklist concept; a representative photograph would be arbitrary and is not required to understand the dictionary entry.
Project turnover process rather than a concrete object; no single subject photograph is required for accurate identification.
Record-drawing concept whose meaning is defined by documentation state, not by the appearance of a unique physical subject.
Request-for-information workflow/document concept; a generic form image would not establish a canonical visual subject.
Contract change-control concept rather than a visually identifiable construction object.
Workplace-organization management practice; no single canonical photograph can represent the concept without becoming illustrative rather than identificatory.
Safety-analysis procedure/document concept; visual identity is not necessary for dictionary recognition.
Work-authorization procedure/document concept; a permit layout varies by organization and is not a stable canonical visual subject.

The canonical is defined by the drawing's record/as-built status rather than one stable visual layout; project drawing formats vary, so a representative photograph would be arbitrary and potentially misleading.
The canonical is a jobsite cleanup/housekeeping practice and slang usage, not a unique physical subject; any photograph would depict an arbitrary cleanup scene rather than identify the term itself.

The canonical is the inspection practice of marking defects, while tape, chalk, tags, symbols, and colors vary by site; a single photograph would depict one arbitrary marking convention rather than identify the concept reliably.

The canonical is a broad dust-control practice combining extraction, wet methods, barriers, ventilation, and housekeeping; no single photograph can represent the concept without privileging one arbitrary control method.
The canonical is the broad jobsite/slang concept 'genba'; any construction-site photograph would be an arbitrary example of a location rather than a stable visual subject for the term itself.

The canonical covers jobsite hand signaling as a communication practice; there are multiple distinct signals, so one photograph would represent only an arbitrary gesture and could misstate the broader concept.

The canonical is a broad work category covering welding, cutting, brazing and other spark/flame-producing operations; one photograph would depict only one arbitrary subtype rather than the concept itself.

The canonical is defined by the inspection information recorded, while form layouts and media vary by organization; a representative document photograph would be arbitrary rather than a stable visual identity.

The canonical is the broad insulation material category spanning fibrous, foam, board, spray and other forms; a single photograph of one subtype would misleadingly narrow the generic concept, while specific insulation canonicals can carry images.
The canonical is a spoken/shouted jobsite warning expression rather than a physical subject; any scene photograph would be arbitrary and would not identify the term itself.

The canonical is the KY hazard-prediction practice/site-safety concept rather than one physical subject; a meeting board, worksheet, or group scene would be an arbitrary implementation and would not identify the concept itself.

The canonical is a diagnostic investigation process that may use visual inspection, water testing, infrared imaging, borescopes, or moisture measurement; one photograph would depict only one arbitrary method rather than the leak-tracing concept.

The canonical is the surveying procedure of measuring elevations and level differences, not a unique physical object; the principal instruments already have separate canonicals, so one equipment photograph would misrepresent the process.

Load-bearing status is a structural function that generally cannot be established reliably from a wall's visible appearance alone; an ordinary wall photograph could be misleading rather than identify the canonical property.

The canonical is the lockout/tagout safety procedure and control system; locks, tags, devices, and isolation arrangements vary, so one photographed setup would be only an arbitrary implementation rather than the procedure itself.

PPE is a broad category covering helmets, gloves, footwear, eye, hearing, respiratory and fall protection; one photograph would arbitrarily represent only a subset, while specific PPE canonicals can carry their own images.

Drainage slope is a geometric condition defined by measured fall toward an outlet; an ordinary photograph cannot reliably establish the slope and would be an arbitrary visual example rather than a stable canonical subject.

Low-E glass is defined primarily by a low-emissivity coating/performance property that is not reliably distinguishable in an ordinary photograph from other glazing; a representative photo would risk asserting an invisible property.

The canonical is an inspection/closeout practice in which defects are marked during a walkthrough; tape color, marking style, and inspected subjects vary by project, so a single photograph would depict an arbitrary instance rather than the practice itself.

The canonical is a recurring safety-inspection activity rather than one stable visual subject; any photograph would show an arbitrary checklist, worker, or site condition rather than identify the practice itself.

The canonical is an inspection procedure for evaluating surface flatness, which may use straightedges, levels, laser methods, or other instruments; one photograph would represent only one arbitrary method rather than the concept.

The canonical is a work-authorization document/process whose form layout, approval workflow, and fields vary by organization; one photograph would be arbitrary and would not identify the concept reliably.
The canonical is an energy-isolation safety procedure spanning locks, tags, devices, and documented steps; a single photograph of one setup would misleadingly narrow the broader practice.
The canonical is a safety-reporting record/process whose form and media vary by organization; a photograph of one report would be an arbitrary template rather than the stable concept.

The canonical is a closeout/defect-list management concept whose document format and workflow vary by project; a single photograph would show only an arbitrary checklist or inspection scene rather than the concept itself.
The canonical is a finish-inspection and defect-identification process; the inspected defects and marking methods vary, so one photograph would depict only an arbitrary example.
The canonical is an inspection procedure for verifying subfloor level/flatness and may use several tools and measurement methods; no single photograph is a stable visual identity for the process.
The canonical is a safety briefing/meeting practice rather than one unique object; any photograph would show an arbitrary group or meeting format and would not identify the concept reliably.

The canonical is a jobsite safety briefing/meeting practice rather than a unique physical subject; any photograph would show an arbitrary group, location, or meeting format rather than the concept itself.
